design_detail: Comprehensive narrative pharmacology review (Pharmacological Reviews 70(3):621-660, July 2018) from a University of Maryland and NIH intramural group. Three parts: clinical uses and side effects with the plasma concentrations reported for them (Table 1); pharmacokinetics of ketamine, its enantiomers and its metabolites in humans and rodents, including unpublished data from the authors (Table 2; Figures 1 and 2 give the metabolic pathways); and pharmacodynamics at NMDA receptors and about fifteen other targets, with reported affinities and potencies collected in Table 3, mostly from rodent tissue, cell lines and oocytes. No search strategy, no selection criteria and no appraisal of the cited studies. The central argument, that hydroxynorketamine metabolites carry part of ketamine's antidepressant action, rests largely on the authors' own rodent work, and most authors hold patents or patent applications on those metabolites. A correction was published in October 2018 (Pharmacol Rev 70(4):879, doi 10.1124/pr.116.015198err) and concerns only the copyright statement.
can_establish: Which primary studies report ketamine's human pharmacokinetics by route, its metabolic pathways and circulating metabolites, and its affinities and potencies at NMDA receptors and other targets, and how those values compare with the plasma concentrations reached in clinical use, as the authors assembled them in 2018.
cannot_establish: Any pharmacokinetic or receptor value with more authority than the primary study it is taken from (there is no systematic search, no appraisal, and several values are the authors' estimates or unpublished); whether ketamine's metabolites contribute to its effects in people (the evidence offered is preclinical); and the safety statements made in passing, for which no evidence is reviewed.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The human data cited come from healthy volunteers (for example White et al., 1985; Krystal et al., 1994; Bowdle et al., 1998; Vollenweider et al., 1997), surgical patients (Geisslinger et al., 1993), children (Grant et al., 1983; Malinovsky et al., 1996; Adamowicz and Kala, 2005; Hornik et al.), patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression (Zarate et al., 2012a; Zhao et al., 2012) and patients with complex regional pain syndrome (Moaddel et al., 2010). The receptor data come mostly from rat and other animal brain tissue and from recombinant receptors in cell lines and oocytes, with a few human post-mortem brain samples (Kornhuber et al., 1989; Oye et al., 1992, two brains; Gilling et al., 2009).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; the studies were chosen by the authors.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is unsystematic and weighted towards the authors' own laboratories for everything about the metabolites (Moaddel et al., 2010, 2013, 2015a, 2015b, 2016; Zarate et al., 2012a; Zhao et al., 2012; Can et al., 2016; Zanos et al., 2016; Morris et al., 2017), including rows of Table 2 marked as unpublished data. The human pharmacokinetic values rest on a small set of mostly older studies, some carried out in children and some designed as drug-interaction studies, and several plasma concentrations are the authors' own estimates from published figures rather than measured values. Studies of deaths and most studies of long-term harm in people who use ketamine are not reviewed, although the review makes general statements about both.

exposure.measurement: Varies by cited study: drug given under laboratory or clinical conditions with plasma or urine concentrations measured by the cited laboratories; radioligand binding, electrophysiology and uptake assays in vitro; positron emission tomography in a few human studies.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as the review reports them. The human metabolite data come from single 40-minute intravenous infusions of 0.5 mg/kg in patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression (Zarate et al., 2012a; Zhao et al., 2012) and from a continuous infusion over five days in complex regional pain syndrome (Moaddel et al., 2010). The comparisons between routes come from Clements et al. (1982), Grant et al. (1981), Yanagihara et al. (2003) and a paediatric study (Malinovsky et al., 1996); the enantiomer comparisons from White et al. (1985), Geisslinger et al. (1993) and Ihmsen et al. (2001). Table 1 collects the doses and plasma concentrations of the cited clinical studies and also lists amounts reported in surveys and case reports of non-medical use; this card does not reproduce those lists.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed for the cited studies. By their titles in the reference list, the two sources given for the roughly 5-hour half-life of S-ketamine are drug-interaction studies of oral S-ketamine (Hagelberg et al., 2010, with clarithromycin; Peltoniemi et al., 2012, with rifampicin), so those values describe control arms of interaction studies.

comparison.controls: Not applicable at review level; the comparisons are between enantiomers, routes, metabolites, species and molecular targets.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a pharmacology review. For the cross-sectional studies of cognition and brain imaging in people who use ketamine that it cites in passing, the review itself says that comorbid and environmental factors are hard to control.

outcomes.instruments: Cited measures: plasma and urine concentrations and the parameters derived from them (Cmax, time to peak, AUC, half-life, clearance, volume of distribution, bioavailability, enantiomer ratios); radioligand binding (Ki or IC50, mostly displacement of [3H]MK-801), electrophysiological potency against evoked currents (IC50), and uptake assays; positron emission tomography of D2 and GABA-A receptor binding in people; rodent behavioural tests of antidepressant-like effects.
outcomes.validity_norms: Values for the same target vary several-fold between laboratories, species, tissues, assays and magnesium conditions (Table 3; values are mean plus or minus standard error unless marked otherwise). The review's working test of whether a target matters is whether its affinity or potency falls within the plasma concentrations reached clinically, which by its own Table 1 are about 0.8 micromolar after an antidepressant infusion and about 5 to 10 micromolar at anaesthesia.
outcomes.operationalization: A target is treated as plausibly relevant when its affinity or potency lies within clinically reached concentrations, taken as up to about 10 micromolar; side effects are framed as dose dependent.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited; the numbers are in the key findings. In summary: bioavailability is given as 93% intramuscular (41% in a paediatric population model), 16% to 29% oral for racemic ketamine and 8% to 11% for oral S-ketamine, 45% to 50% intranasal and 25% to 30% rectal; plasma protein binding 10% to 50%; steady-state volume of distribution 3 to 5 l/kg; elimination half-life 2 to 4 hours in adults, with children about twice as fast. After a 40-minute intravenous infusion of 0.5 mg/kg in treatment-resistant major depression, peak plasma concentrations were 204.13 plus or minus 101.46 ng/ml for ketamine at 40 minutes, 73.54 plus or minus 31.86 ng/ml for norketamine at 80 minutes, 13.27 plus or minus 6.92 ng/ml for dehydronorketamine at 110 minutes and 23.19 plus or minus 11.88 ng/ml for (2R,6R;2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine at 230 minutes. At the NMDA receptor, reported Ki values span 0.18 to 3.1 micromolar for racemic ketamine, with S-ketamine about four times more potent than R-ketamine, and the estimated maximum receptor occupancy after the antidepressant infusion is 31% plus or minus 18%. Most other targets act at 10 to 1000 micromolar. No pooling, no intervals and no statistical synthesis anywhere.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration; none would be expected for a narrative review, and none is claimed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. Evidence against the hydroxynorketamine account appears only as a parenthetical pointer to two papers, while the authors' own published replies to critiques are cited as support without the critiques' arguments being described. Several affinity ranges in the text leave out values listed in the review's own Table 3, in each case values that would weaken the contrast being drawn (see reporting issues).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The cited evidence places ketamine's best-characterised action at the NMDA receptor, with affinities of roughly 0.2 to 3 micromolar in rodent and human brain tissue and S-ketamine about four times as potent as R-ketamine, within the plasma concentrations reached at anaesthetic and subanaesthetic doses, while most other targets need 10 to 1000 micromolar. Human pharmacokinetics rest on a handful of studies: high intramuscular, intermediate intranasal and low oral bioavailability, an elimination half-life of 2 to 4 hours in adults, extensive metabolism to norketamine and then to dehydronorketamine and hydroxynorketamines, and metabolite concentrations measured in depressed patients by the authors' group. The proposal that hydroxynorketamines carry antidepressant activity rests on rodent experiments, almost all from the authors' laboratories.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract describes the metabolite evidence as preclinical, which matches the text. Elsewhere the review makes statements that the text does not support. It says most if not all side effects are dose dependent, transient and self-resolving, citing three studies of therapeutic use, a few lines after its own account of bladder damage and lasting memory deficits with prolonged non-medical use. It states that the authors know of no report of a lethal dose in humans and that deaths from ketamine alone are very rare, without reviewing any death-register or coronial study (its sources here are a forensic case series and a review). It says repeated administration prolongs elimination, from urinary detection windows after three infusions described in what reads as a single person. In Future Directions it calls clinical work with the metabolites feasible given the historical safety knowledge on ketamine, which assumes the metabolites inherit ketamine's safety record. Most authors hold patents or patent applications on the metabolites the review presents as drug candidates.

timeline.event: Clements, Nimmo and Grant: bioavailability and pharmacokinetics by intravenous, intramuscular and oral routes; the review's source for intramuscular bioavailability and for the comparison of half-life and clearance between routes.
White et al.: comparative pharmacology of the ketamine isomers in volunteers (elimination half-lives of 155 to 158 minutes for the separate enantiomers; relative anaesthetic potency), as cited.
Oye, Paulsen and Maurset: displacement of [3H]MK-801 in two human post-mortem brains, among the few human binding data in Table 3.
Geisslinger et al.: enantiomer pharmacokinetics in surgical patients; no interconversion between enantiomers in vivo, as cited.
Krystal et al.: subanaesthetic effects in healthy volunteers, the review's main source for dissociative, psychotomimetic and cognitive effects.
Malhotra et al.: effects of ketamine on human cognition, cited among the memory studies.
Vollenweider et al.: differential psychopathology of S- and R-ketamine in healthy volunteers, summarised here with its plasma levels.
Newcomer et al.: ketamine-induced memory impairment and psychosis, cited among the memory studies.
Ihmsen et al.: R-ketamine inhibits the elimination of S-ketamine, the review's source for the clearance difference between the single enantiomer and the racemate.
Yanagihara et al.: plasma ketamine and norketamine after different preparations in healthy Japanese volunteers, one of the two sources for intranasal and rectal bioavailability.

Zarate et al. (2012a) and Zhao et al. (2012): plasma ketamine and metabolite profiles after a 40-minute 0.5 mg/kg infusion in depressed patients, from the authors' group; the source of this review's human metabolite numbers.
Morgan and Curran for the Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs: review of ketamine use, cited here for non-medical use, dependence and cognitive effects.

Zanos et al. (Nature): antidepressant actions of hydroxynorketamines without NMDA receptor inhibition in mice, from the authors' group; critiques followed in 2017 and the authors' replies are cited here.
Peltoniemi et al.: review of clinical pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, cited here for plasma protein binding; a later secondary source on the same clinical literature.
This review; a correction in October 2018 (Pharmacol Rev 70(4):879) changed only the copyright statement.

replication.where_it_stands: A widely used secondary source for ketamine pharmacology. Its human pharmacokinetic figures should be cited from the primary studies, several of which are carded in this round (clements_1982, yanagihara_2003), and peltoniemi_2016 is a later review of the same clinical literature. Its receptor tables are an index of preclinical values, each to be checked in the primary paper. The review cites no human study in which a hydroxynorketamine was given, and states that no clinical study of R-ketamine in depressed patients had been published and that no study had compared the enantiomers with each other or with the racemate in people, so its metabolite and enantiomer arguments were preclinical when written.

(Footnotes).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (Footnotes): the authors declare competing financial interests. R.M. and C.A.Z. are listed as coinventors on a patent for the use of (2R,6R)-hydroxynorketamine, (S)-dehydronorketamine and other stereoisomeric dehydro and hydroxylated metabolites of (R,S)-ketamine in the treatment of depression and neuropathic pain. P.Z., R.M., P.J.M., C.J.T., C.A.Z. and T.D.G. are listed as coinventors on a patent application for the use of (2R,6R)-hydroxynorketamine and (2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine in the treatment of depression, anxiety, anhedonia, suicidal ideation and post-traumatic stress disorders. R.M., P.J.M., C.A.Z. and C.J.T. have assigned their patent rights to the US government but will share a percentage of any royalties the government receives; P.Z. and T.D.G. have assigned their patent rights to the University of Maryland, Baltimore, but will share a percentage of any royalties the university receives. All other authors declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Maryland School of Medicine (psychiatry, pharmacology, anatomy and neurobiology, epidemiology and public health, and medicine) and three NIH intramural programs. The review's central argument concerns compounds on which most of its authors hold patents or patent applications, and much of the supporting evidence comes from their own laboratories, including data marked unpublished. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: For the metabolite question: human studies measuring ketamine and its metabolites in cerebrospinal fluid or brain alongside clinical effects, and randomised placebo-controlled trials of a hydroxynorketamine with measured plasma levels. For pharmacokinetics: crossover studies in adults in which the same people receive each route, with enantiomer-specific and metabolite-specific assays and sampling long enough to define the terminal half-life, so that bioavailability and half-life no longer rest on small older studies, studies in children, or the control arms of drug-interaction studies.

domains.note: No search, no dates, no criteria; the authors chose the evidence.

Caveats appear in places (many findings not validated by independent laboratories; a low-dose antidepressant finding awaiting replication; cross-sectional studies unable to control comorbidity; baseline behavioural differences in knockout mice; species differences in pharmacokinetics), but single values, unpublished data and the authors’ own estimates of plasma concentrations are presented without appraisal. The review also draws ranges from its own Table 3 in a way that mixes Ki with IC50 values and leaves out tabulated values, each time in the direction of the contrast it is drawing (reporting issue 3), which is a failure of appraisal of its own assembled evidence and not only of the primary studies.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The metabolite pharmacokinetics and pharmacology rest largely on the authors' laboratories and on unpublished data, on compounds most of them have patented.

Hypotheses are usually flagged and preclinical evidence is labelled as such, but the general safety statements and the claim that clinical work with the metabolites is feasible on ketamine's safety record go beyond the cited evidence.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against the hydroxynorketamine account of ketamine's antidepressant action (evidence against it under-represented)
domains.note: Counter-evidence appears only as a parenthetical pointer to two papers, the authors' replies to critiques are cited without the critiques, and the harms literature is summarised briefly and with reassuring generalisations.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3), so the editors' checklist is used. The review is detailed and generally careful to label preclinical evidence, but its selection is unsystematic, its metabolite sections rest on the authors' own work on compounds they have patented, and evidence against their account is under-represented. It may be cited as a pointer to the primary pharmacokinetic and receptor studies and for its overview of which targets fall within clinically reached concentrations, with every number taken from the primary study it names. It should not be cited for the safety statements, for which it reviews no evidence, nor as evidence that the metabolites act in people.

key_findings.finding: Metabolic pathway: ketamine is first N-demethylated to norketamine, mainly by the liver enzymes CYP2B6 and CYP3A4, and the reaction is stereoselective, since CYP3A4 demethylates S-ketamine faster than R-ketamine while CYP2B6 acts on both about equally (Portmann et al., 2010). Norketamine is then hydroxylated, chiefly by CYP2A6 and CYP2B6, to hydroxynorketamines, or converted to dehydronorketamine by CYP2B6 or by non-enzymatic dehydration of a 5-hydroxynorketamine; minor routes give hydroxyketamines and hydroxyphenyl metabolites. The review attributes part of the variability between people to differences in P450 expression (Hijazi and Boulieu, 2002).
key_findings.locator: II. Pharmacokinetics > A. Metabolism, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Figure 1 and Figure 2 legends

key_findings.finding: Circulating metabolites in people: after a single 40-minute intravenous infusion of 0.5 mg/kg, norketamine, dehydronorketamine and (2R,6R;2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine were the major plasma metabolites in treatment-resistant bipolar depression (Zhao et al., 2012) and in unipolar and bipolar depression (Zarate et al., 2012a), all detectable from 40 minutes after the end of the infusion. Estimated mean times to peak were about 1.33 hours for the norketamine enantiomers and about 3.83 hours for the dehydronorketamine enantiomers and (2R,6R;2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine. S to R ratios 40 to 230 minutes after the infusion were 0.84 for ketamine, 1.0 for norketamine and 0.67 for dehydronorketamine (Zhao et al., 2012); comparable ratios cited elsewhere are 0.91 for ketamine in surgical patients (Geisslinger et al., 1993) and 0.77, 0.71 and 0.71 during a five-day infusion in complex regional pain syndrome (Moaddel et al., 2010).
key_findings.locator: II. Pharmacokinetics > A. Metabolism, 4th paragraph; II. Pharmacokinetics > C. Distribution, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Peak plasma concentrations after the same 40-minute 0.5 mg/kg infusion (Zarate et al., 2012a), mean plus or minus standard deviation. In treatment-resistant major depression: ketamine 204.13 plus or minus 101.46 ng/ml (0.86 plus or minus 0.43 micromolar) at 40 minutes; norketamine 73.54 plus or minus 31.86 ng/ml at 80 minutes; dehydronorketamine 13.27 plus or minus 6.92 ng/ml at 110 minutes; (2R,6R;2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine 23.19 plus or minus 11.88 ng/ml at 230 minutes. In treatment-resistant bipolar depression: ketamine 177.23 plus or minus 53.8 ng/ml at 40 minutes, norketamine 69.96 plus or minus 19.98 ng/ml at 80 minutes, dehydronorketamine 50.5 plus or minus 27.44 ng/ml at 110 minutes and (2R,6R;2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine 37.59 plus or minus 14.23 ng/ml. Table 2 adds the areas under the curve for the two patient groups (ketamine 873.5 and 975.4 h.ng/ml; the hydroxynorketamine pair 1038 and 1366 h.ng/ml), so total exposure to that metabolite pair exceeded exposure to ketamine itself.
key_findings.locator: II. Pharmacokinetics > A. Metabolism, 5th paragraph; Table 2, Humans rows
key_findings.note: Table 2’s human rows are sourced to ’Zarate et al. (2012a)’ and ’Unpublished data’, so the areas under the curve that carry the comparison between the hydroxynorketamine pair and ketamine itself are partly unpublished and cannot be traced to a primary paper.

key_findings.finding: Absorption and bioavailability by route, as collected by the review: intramuscular 93% with peak concentrations 5 to 30 minutes after dosing (Clements et al., 1982), against 41% in a paediatric population pharmacokinetic analysis (Hornik et al.); oral 16% to 29% with peak concentrations at 20 to 120 minutes, limited by extensive first-pass metabolism; oral S-ketamine 8% to 11% (Peltoniemi et al., 2012; Fanta et al., 2015), consistent with greater first-pass metabolism of that enantiomer; intranasal 45% to 50% and rectal 25% to 30% (Malinovsky et al., 1996; Yanagihara et al., 2003). The review notes that the intranasal route is not subject to first-pass metabolism.

Distribution: ketamine distributes rapidly into well-perfused tissue including brain, with plasma protein binding between 10% and 50% and a steady-state volume of distribution of 3 to 5 l/kg (sources cited include Peltoniemi et al., 2012 and 2016, and Karch and Drummer, 2015). The enantiomers do not interconvert in the body (Geisslinger et al., 1993; Ihmsen et al., 2001). The review states that brain concentrations of ketamine and its metabolites in people are not known, so human brain exposure is inferred only from rodent data.
key_findings.locator: II. Pharmacokinetics > C. Distribution, 1st paragraph; II. Pharmacokinetics > D. Elimination, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: Elimination: high clearance and a short elimination half-life of 2 to 4 hours in adults (Clements et al., 1982; White et al., 1985; Domino, 2010). Terminal half-life and clearance did not differ materially between the intravenous and intramuscular routes in Clements et al. (1982): 186 minutes and 19.1 ml/min per kg intravenously against 155 minutes and 23.2 ml/min per kg intramuscularly. Renal excretion accounts for little unchanged drug, with figures of about 2% ketamine, 2% norketamine and 16% dehydronorketamine, and about 80% excreted as glucuronide conjugates of hydroxyketamine and hydroxynorketamine in urine and bile (Dinis-Oliveira, 2017). Ketamine was undetectable in plasma within a day of a 0.5 mg/kg infusion, whereas dehydronorketamine and the hydroxynorketamine pair were still measurable for up to three days (Zarate et al., 2012a; Zhao et al., 2012). Children eliminate ketamine about twice as fast as adults (Haas and Harper, 1992). S-ketamine given alone has a half-life of about 5 hours and a clearance of 26.3 plus or minus 3.5 ml/kg per minute, against 14.8 plus or minus 1.7 for the same enantiomer within the racemate, which the review reads as inhibition of S-ketamine clearance by R-ketamine (Ihmsen et al., 2001).
key_findings.locator: II. Pharmacokinetics > D. Elimination, 1st to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: NMDA receptor: ketamine is a non-competitive open-channel blocker at the phencyclidine site within the channel pore, with a trapping capability of about 86%, against more than 98% for phencyclidine and 100% for MK-801. Reported affinities for racemic ketamine in the presence of magnesium span Ki 0.18 to 3.1 micromolar across about twenty studies, including human cortex values of 0.42 plus or minus 0.03 (Kornhuber et al., 1989) and 0.67 plus or minus 0.15 micromolar (Gilling et al., 2009). S-ketamine has roughly four times the affinity of R-ketamine and twice that of the racemate (S-ketamine Ki 0.3 to 0.69, R-ketamine 1.4 to 2.57 micromolar), consistent with its greater anaesthetic potency. Subunit selectivity depends on magnesium: without magnesium ketamine blocks GluN1/2A and GluN1/2B somewhat more potently, while at 1 millimolar magnesium it blocks GluN1/2C and GluN1/2D more potently (Kotermanski and Johnson, 2009), and one study found no subunit differences at all (Yamakura et al., 1993), which the review presents as unresolved.
key_findings.locator: III. Pharmacodynamics > A. N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptors, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Table 3, NMDAR rows
key_findings.note: Table 3’s header states that values are mean plus or minus standard error unless marked otherwise, so the two human cortex figures are Ki 0.42 (SE 0.03) and 0.67 (SE 0.15). The racemic rows span rat tissue (cortex, brain, striatum, spinal cord, forebrain, cerebellum, synaptic membranes, cultured neurons), mouse brain, guinea pig brain, dog brain and dog cortex, HEK293 and tsA201 cells and receptors expressed in frog oocytes, beside the two human cortex rows. The review does not describe those two rows as post-mortem; it uses that word only of the separate human brain homogenates that gave the enantiomer values (Oye et al., 1992), whose Table 3 rows add that only two brain samples were used.

key_findings.finding: Receptor occupancy: the subanaesthetic antidepressant regimen (40-minute intravenous infusion of 0.5 mg/kg) was estimated to produce a maximum NMDA receptor occupancy of 31% plus or minus 18%, close to the 32% plus or minus 6% estimated for an antidepressant-relevant dose in rats (10 mg/kg intraperitoneally), both figures taken from Shaffer et al. (2014). The review reports the two estimates side by side and then turns to the antidepressant potency of R-ketamine as the challenge to an account resting on NMDA receptor block alone.
key_findings.locator: III. Pharmacodynamics > A. N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptors, 3rd paragraph (the first running paragraph after Table 3)
key_findings.note: The review prints both spreads without saying whether they are standard deviations or standard errors (Table 3’s header says standard error, Table 2’s says standard deviation), so neither should be cited as an SD. Both are estimates from a cited study, not measurements made here.

key_findings.finding: Metabolites at the NMDA receptor: norketamine also blocks the receptor, with S-norketamine reported at Ki 1.70 to 2.25 micromolar and R-norketamine about eight times weaker (13.0 to 26.46 micromolar) (Ebert et al., 1997; Moaddel et al., 2013). Dehydronorketamine and the hydroxynorketamines are weak or inactive: (2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine displaces [3H]MK-801 only at about 10 to 21 micromolar, while (2R,6R)-hydroxynorketamine does not bind appreciably (Ki above 100 micromolar), and neither inhibits NMDA-evoked currents at concentrations up to 10 micromolar (Zanos et al., 2016, with Suzuki et al., 2017, for the (2R,6R) form; Morris et al., 2017, is a binding study, not a current recording). At 50 micromolar, a concentration the review calls higher than antidepressant-relevant, (2R,6R)-hydroxynorketamine inhibited NMDA-mediated currents by about 40% against more than 90% for ketamine in the same experiment (Suzuki et al., 2017).
key_findings.locator: III. Pharmacodynamics > A. N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptors, 6th and 7th paragraphs; Table 3, norKET, DHNK and HNK rows

key_findings.finding: Other targets, and where the review places them against the concentrations reached in people (about 0.8 micromolar after the antidepressant infusion and about 5 to 10 micromolar at anaesthesia, by its own Table 1). Most tabulated values lie at about 10 to 1000 micromolar, but the review itself treats several as within reach. Nicotinic receptors: alpha4beta4 blocked at IC50 0.24 micromolar in oocytes (Flood and Krasowski, 2000, chicken receptors, complete inhibition at 10 micromolar), alpha3beta4 at 3.1 micromolar and alpha7 at about 17 to 20 micromolar (Coates and Flood, 2001; Moaddel et al., 2013), with the review stating that concentrations up to about 10 micromolar are within the clinically relevant range, so some subtypes may act in people; Table 3 adds dehydronorketamine at the alpha7 receptor at IC50 0.055 micromolar (Moaddel et al., 2013, rat receptors in cells), which the review offers as a possible non-NMDA route for a metabolite. HCN1 channels inhibited at EC50 8.2 to 15.6 micromolar for the racemate and 4.1 to 7.4 for S-ketamine (Chen et al., 2009), which the review links to anaesthesia, citing the suppression of ketamine anaesthesia in HCN knockout mice. Muscarinic M1 reported both at Ki 45 micromolar in cells (Hirota et al., 2002) and at IC50 5.7 micromolar in oocytes (Durieux, 1995), the lower value described by the review as a clinically relevant concentration and the discrepancy attributed to the expression system. Opioid receptors in the tens to hundreds of micromolar, with S-ketamine the higher-affinity enantiomer; sigma receptors at 19 to 139 micromolar in the text, with R-ketamine the higher-affinity enantiomer (but see reporting issues for the tabulated racemic Ki of 0.15). Monoamine transporters mostly above 60 micromolar, with lower tabulated values of IC50 4.6 micromolar for the dopamine transporter (Keita et al., 1996, rat striatum) and 18.8 and 20.2 micromolar for the serotonin transporter (Martin et al., 1988, 1990); voltage-gated sodium channels and L-type calcium channels at hundreds of micromolar to millimolar in most preparations, with a tabulated L-type calcium IC50 of 9.2 micromolar in frog myocytes; GABA-A effects only at hundreds of micromolar, and no binding at subanaesthetic doses in a human positron emission tomography study (Salmi et al., 2005). The review concludes that ketamine has lower affinity for these targets than for NMDA receptors and that many of the reported findings have not been validated by independent laboratories.
key_findings.locator: III. Pharmacodynamics, introductory paragraph; sections B to I; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Dopamine: ketamine was reported as a high-affinity D2 partial agonist (Ki 0.055 to 1.0 micromolar; EC50 0.9 plus or minus 0.4 micromolar; Kapur and Seeman, 2001, 2002; Seeman et al., 2005), an action proposed to underlie psychotomimetic effects, and three human imaging studies reported reduced striatal D2 binding after subanaesthetic dosing (Breier et al., 1998; Smith et al., 1998; Vollenweider et al., 2000). The review sets against this two human imaging studies that found no change in striatal D2 availability (Kegeles et al., 2002; Aalto et al., 2002), a human study in which a D2 antagonist did not block ketamine's psychotomimetic effects (Krystal and D'Souza, 2001), and a study finding no functional activity at any dopamine receptor subtype up to 10 micromolar and no change in evoked dopamine release in mice (Can et al., 2016).
key_findings.locator: III. Pharmacodynamics > E. Monoaminergic Receptors and Transporters, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The metabolite account is preclinical as presented: hydroxynorketamines are reported to produce antidepressant-like behaviour in rodents without the sensory dissociation, ataxia or self-administration seen with ketamine (Zanos et al., 2016), and R-ketamine is reported to be a more potent and longer-lasting antidepressant than S-ketamine across rodent tests over a 30-fold dose range, with no difference in brain exposure between enantiomers. The review states that no clinical study of R-ketamine in depressed patients had been published and that no clinical study had compared the enantiomers with each other or with the racemate.
key_findings.locator: IV. Conclusions > A. (R)- and (S)-Ketamine as Antidepressants, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; IV. Conclusions > B. Utility of Ketamine's Hydroxynorketamine Metabolites as Drug Treatments, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Neurotoxicity, as summarised: neuronal vacuolation (Olney lesions) in rats occurs after high doses of 40 to 60 mg/kg subcutaneously but not after 5 to 20 mg/kg, doses far above those used for analgesia or antidepressant effect, and at low doses the changes reverse within 24 hours. In non-human primates given 1 mg/kg daily intravenously, reduced white matter integrity was reported after 3 months and increased prefrontal cell death after 6 months; hyperphosphorylated tau was reported in monkeys and mice dosed daily for 3 to 6 months. The human evidence cited is two cross-sectional imaging studies in people who use ketamine (cortical atrophy, Wang et al., 2013; loss of frontal white matter integrity correlated with lifetime use, Liao et al., 2010), and the review calls the relevance of the animal lesions to people controversial and difficult to assess.
key_findings.locator: I. Introduction > B. Side Effects > 4. Neurotoxicity, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Side effects in people, as the review collates them from the cited studies: dissociation and positive and negative psychotomimetic symptoms emerging within 10 minutes of the start of a 40-minute 0.5 mg/kg infusion and subsiding within 40 minutes of its end, with little or no such effect at 0.1 mg/kg (Krystal et al., 1994); impaired vigilance, verbal fluency and delayed recall during and immediately after the infusion, with global cognitive function and immediate recall preserved (Krystal et al., 1994); exacerbation of psychotic symptoms in patients with schizophrenia (Lahti et al., 2001; Malhotra et al., 1997); dizziness, nausea and vomiting, tachycardia and raised blood pressure, mild respiratory depression, and ocular and musculoskeletal effects; and, with prolonged non-medical use, urological complications including ulcerative cystitis (Shahani et al., 2007; Chu et al., 2008) and lasting memory deficits (Morgan et al., 2006; Morgan and Curran, 2012; Zhang et al., 2018).
key_findings.locator: I. Introduction > B. Side Effects > 1. Psychoactive Effects (a to c), 2. Direct and Indirect Peripheral Effects and 3. Long-Term Effects

reporting_issues.issue: Unit conversion error in the elimination section: urinary concentrations in children are given as 0.1 to 1442 ng/ml (0.0004 to 0.031 micromolar) for norketamine, but 1442 ng/ml of norketamine (molecular weight about 224) is about 6.4 micromolar, not 0.031 (editors' calculation). The ketamine figures in the same sentence (2 to 1204 ng/ml, 0.008 to 5.06 micromolar) convert correctly.
reporting_issues.consequence: The micromolar range printed for norketamine is wrong by more than two orders of magnitude; only the ng/ml values should be cited, and from the primary study (Adamowicz and Kala, 2005).

reporting_issues.issue: The same stereoisomer pair is listed twice as the two major metabolites in a patient receiving a five-day infusion: the sentence names (2R,6R;2S,6S)- and (2R,6R;2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamines, where the second is presumably the (2S,6R;2R,6S) pair named earlier in the section.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader cannot tell from this review which two hydroxynorketamine pairs predominated during prolonged infusion; the primary paper (Moaddel et al., 2010) must be read.

reporting_issues.issue: Text and Table 2 disagree on one dispersion value: the mouse plasma peak concentration of ketamine is given in the text as 2.36 plus or minus 0.18 micromolar and in Table 2 as 2.36 plus or minus 0.36, with the same ng/ml value (561.89 plus or minus 86.09) in both.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, and preclinical, but it shows the tables and text were not reconciled.

reporting_issues.issue: Affinity ranges in the text omit values printed in the review's own Table 3, each time in the direction that strengthens the contrast drawn. The text gives S-norketamine Ki 1.70 to 2.25 and R-norketamine 13.0 to 26.46 micromolar (an eight-fold difference), while Table 3 also lists 0.87 and 0.60 micromolar respectively (Morris et al., 2017), which would remove the difference. The text gives (2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine Ki 10.4 to 21.0 micromolar, but 10.4 is an IC50 in Table 3 and the lowest tabulated Ki is 7.34. The dehydronorketamine ranges (59.7 to 74.6 for the R form, 39.0 to 42.0 for the S form) likewise mix Ki with IC50 values and omit the tabulated Ki of 29.7 for the S form.
reporting_issues.consequence: Ranges quoted from the text may be narrower or higher than the tabulated evidence, and Ki and IC50 values are mixed within a single range; claims about metabolite affinity should cite the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: Internal inconsistency about the lower dose in Krystal et al. (1994): one section says little to no psychoactive effect was seen at 0.1 mg/kg, another says the same dose produced mild euphoria.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review cannot be cited for what the lower dose did; the primary study (carded as sc_krystal_1994) settles it.

reporting_issues.issue: Several plasma concentrations attributed to primary studies are the review's own estimates, flagged in the text with wording such as estimated or calculated from, including the 100 to 250 ng/ml range for the Krystal et al. (1994) infusion, which is printed in Table 1 beside measured values without that qualification.
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 mixes measured and estimated concentrations; any concentration taken from it must be checked in the primary paper before it is cited as measured.

reporting_issues.issue: The opioid section reports that naloxone augmented the dissociative and cognitive effects of ketamine in healthy volunteers, citing Krystal et al. (2006), whose title in the reference list names naltrexone, not naloxone.
reporting_issues.consequence: The drug named in the text does not match the cited source; a claim about opioid-antagonist interaction must be taken from the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The paediatric population pharmacokinetic study is cited in the text as Hornik et al. (2013) but appears in the reference list as 2018.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor citation error; it affects the figure of 41% intramuscular bioavailability, which should be traced to the correct paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Units error in the account of the enantiomer study: average plasma ketamine levels are printed as 379 plus or minus 71 ng/mg and 389 plus or minus 74 ng/mg, where the accompanying micromolar values show that ng/ml is meant.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the micromolar values are internally consistent (editors' check) and the primary study (carded as sc_vollenweider_1997a) holds the measured values.

reporting_issues.issue: General safety statements are made without a supporting body of evidence: that deaths from ketamine alone are very rare and that no report of a lethal dose in humans is known to the authors, sourced to a forensic case series and a review, and that most if not all side effects are dose dependent, transient and self-resolving, sourced to three studies of therapeutic use.
reporting_issues.consequence: These sentences must not be cited as evidence about deaths or about the persistence of harms; the encyclopedia's death and long-term-harm claims rest on registry and cohort studies instead.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 attributes the antidepressant row (0.5 mg/kg as a 40-minute intravenous infusion; 185 ng/ml; 0.78 micromolar) to Zarate et al. (2006), while the text states that the value was calculated from Zarate et al. (2012a).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1; I. Introduction > A. Clinical Therapeutic Effects > 3. Antidepressant, last paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader is pointed to the wrong paper for the single most-cited concentration in the review; the figure is the review’s own calculation and should be traced to Zarate et al. (2012a).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3’s sigma-receptor rows are inconsistent with the text: Hustveit et al. (1995) is tabulated with a racemic Ki of 0.15 micromolar, while the text reports 19 micromolar for the R form and 131 for the S form from the same study. A racemate cannot bind about a hundred times more strongly than either of its enantiomers (editors’ reading).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3, sigma rows; III. Pharmacodynamics > F. Sigma Receptors
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two sigma figures must be wrong, and the tabulated 0.15 micromolar sits far outside the 19 to 139 micromolar range the text gives; no sigma value should be cited from this review without the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence carrying the racemic NMDA-receptor range of Ki 0.18 to 3.1 micromolar cites three sources with no matching racemic row in Table 3 (MacDonald et al., 1987, which has no row at all; Moaddel et al., 2013, and Bonifazi et al., 2015, which appear only under the enantiomers), and Table 3 carries a racemic Ki above 10 micromolar (Georg and Friedl, 1991, in a rat glioma hybrid cell line) that falls outside the stated range without comment.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, III. Pharmacodynamics > A. N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptors, 2nd paragraph; Table 3, NMDAR rows
reporting_issues.consequence: The range cannot be audited against the table, and it is narrower than the tabulated values; affinities should be taken from the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: Tissue mismatch between text and table for norketamine: the text locates the S-norketamine Ki range in the spinal cord and the cerebral cortex, while Table 3’s two matching rows are rat cortex (Ebert et al., 1997) and rat whole brain (Moaddel et al., 2013), with no spinal-cord norketamine row.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, III. Pharmacodynamics > A. N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptors, 6th paragraph; Table 3, norketamine rows
reporting_issues.consequence: The tissue in which a metabolite affinity was measured cannot be taken from this review.
